The value assigned by the Applicant and FPC staff to the fishing recreation generated by the stream system is insignificant in relation to the habitats unreplaceable value to the citizens of South Carolina. The flooding of Lakes Keowee and Jocassee destroyed approximately 25 percent of all trout waters in South Carolina. With this impoundment many of the highest quality fisheries in the State were destroyed. The entire Keowee River drainage including the Thompson, Whitewater, Horsepasture and Toxaway Rivers simply do not exist except as small remnants in South Carolina any longer. The remaining "Keowee River" drainages are impacted by sediment from project construction and timber harvest practices which have degraded the quality of these habitats. The Little and Big Eastatoe, Bearcamp, Thompson and Cane Creek drainages are severely degraded, to mention only a few of the more prominent. It is for these reasons that the Howard creek drainage with its native stream and spawning run fisheries have so much more value than the Applicant's analysis would indicate.
The excellent trout fishery which has developed in Lake Jocassee and its tributaries has become a valuable resource to the citizens of South Carolina. The proposed project has admitted negative impacts which could jeopardize the very existence of the delicate dissolved oxygen budget and stratification of the lake which supports this second story fishery.
A definite conflict over the use of our regions unique and valuable resources has thus developed between the citizens of Upper Scuth Carolina and the Applicant. The major problem then resolves itself into a question of values or goals for these conflicting groups. It is recognized that the proposed project offers significant capital and operating expense advantages over the several alternate sources of this power. An examination of the cost associated with these alternate sources indicates that this development offers only a small incremental saving in cost per kilowatt hour to the actual consumer. The conclusion, therefore, is that the project has mainly economic benefits to the Applicant in terms of capital cost per kilowatt, but only small savings to the citizens of our area. As citizens, it is this incremental cost which must be weighed against the negative costs of resource loss. The Keowee-Toxaway complex in recent months has been responsible for the generation of over 40 percent of the total Duke production.
